title: How the band ended: tax threat and losses
summary: Willard Alexander wanted a dance band; the tax at the gate ended it.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: Did we say how we stopped it?
You mentioned you had back problems?
Were we on tape when we did that?
I believe so, but let's talk about it a little more. We kind of said it in passing.

Ever since the first time out, we began losing money and it was suggested from the agency, Willard Alexander agency, that we cut down the size of the band and stop playing what we're doing and play dance music. I'm sure that Miller's getting that too, that's the only thing he knows when it comes down to that. But we wouldn't do that, there would be no purpose. I wouldn't do it today; there is no purpose at all in doing it that way. So we said (inaudible) so that we can at least break even, so it doesn't
keep on adding up that way, and that was the end of the band.

One of the things that precipitated it was the government tax, and they were threatening to take it at the gate, which means nobody would get anything, so why get all the way out in the boondocks and have no money and how were we going to get home. That would have been worse than stopping it when we did.
I think it was probably the right thing to do.
You kept the band going as a recording group for a while.
Yes, as long as the contract lasted. Victor finally decided they didn't want any more of it and stopped it.
Don Costa got the idea we should try something for United Artists, which we hadn't done, but we did it. But that's the last, from then on it was nothing.
If they did sell anything, they didn't let us know. I've never seen a statement from them.
